extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in complex analysis; practitioners using contour integration and residue methods
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and global theorems for evaluating definite real integrals (and related complex integrals) using contour integration, the Residue Theorem, and the global Cauchy theory in simply connected regions. Includes contour choices (semicircles, rectangles), handling poles on the real axis, branch choices for log and powers, and estimates for arc integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue Theorem (general form)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a region except for isolated poles z_j and a piecewise C^1 cycle Γ does not pass through any of the poles, then ∮_Γ f(z) dz = 2πi Σ_j Res f(z_j) n(Γ, z_j), only finitely many terms being nonzero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires f meromorphic in region bounded by the curve; n(Γ,z_j) is the winding number. The proof and application assume the curve avoids poles; essential singularities complicate residue definition. (Examples show using this to evaluate real integrals by choosing appropriate contours.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue Theorem for a simple closed curve oriented with inside on left
rubrics_metrics.description: When Γ is a simple closed curve oriented so interior is on the left, n(Γ, z_j)=1 for poles inside and 0 for poles outside, so ∮_Γ f(z) dz = 2πi × sum of residues at poles inside Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the usual practical form used in contour integrals: choose a contour that encloses exactly the poles whose residues contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contour method for ∫_{−∞}^{∞} P(x)/Q(x) dx (degree condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate ∫_{−∞}^{∞} P(x)/Q(x) dx by closing the contour with a large semicircle, require Q(x) nowhere 0 on the real axis and deg Q − deg P ≥ 2 (equivalently deg P ≤ deg Q − 2) so that the integral over the large semicircle tends to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the degree condition holds, the semicircle contribution vanishes as radius R→∞; then the real integral equals 2πi times sum of residues in the chosen half-plane. Exact factorization of Q helps compute residues; simple poles simplify residue computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use e^{iz} (or e^{iux}) in place of cos z to ensure decay
rubrics_metrics.description: When integrands involve cos x or sin x, replace cos z by e^{iz} (or use e^{iux}) so that in the upper half-plane e^{iz} decays (and similarly choose lower half-plane depending on sign of exponent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick semicircle in upper half-plane for integrands decaying there (e^{iz} for Im z > 0), and in lower half-plane for the opposite sign. This ensures the arc integral goes to 0 if exponential factor decays in that half-plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contour choice depends on sign of Fourier-type exponent u
rubrics_metrics.description: For integrals of the form ∫ e^{iux} P(x)/Q(x) dx, choose the closing contour (upper vs lower half-plane) according to the sign of u so that e^{iux} decays on the arc, enabling the arc integral to vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either semicircle or rectangle contours can be used; for u>0 close in upper half-plane, for u<0 close in lower half-plane. Both choices work when u=0 only if arc integrals vanish by polynomial-degree arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling non-absolutely-convergent integrals via rectangular contours
rubrics_metrics.description: When the integral is not absolutely convergent (e.g., integrands like e^{ix}/x), use rectangular contours with vertical sides at X1 and X2 and let X1,X2→±∞; include small semicircles around poles on the real axis to treat singularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique yields limits of integrals on finite segments first, then passes to X1,X2→∞. One typically obtains Cauchy principal values for integrals with poles on the real axis, with small semicircles contributing characteristic terms (e.g., ±πi times residue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poles on the real axis give principal-value contributions (simple poles)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are finitely many simple poles on the real axis and finitely many poles in the upper half-plane, then ∫_{−∞}^{∞} e^{ix} P(x)/Q(x) dx equals 2πi times sum of residues in the open upper half-plane plus πi times the sum of residues at simple poles on the real axis, with the integral interpreted as a Cauchy principal value at each real pole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factor πi for real simple poles arises from taking half the contribution when the contour indents around the pole; principal-value integrals (PV) are used. Examples show PV ∫ e^{ix}/x dx = πi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double (or higher-order) poles on real axis can prevent finite limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When a pole on the real axis has order ≥2 (e.g., a double pole), the limiting process of shrinking indentations may not give a finite limit; the method that yields PV for simple poles may fail and divergences can appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate that for a double pole the contribution from small semicircles need not tend to a finite value as the indentation radius → 0; treat higher-order real-axis poles with caution or use alternate regularization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a branch of log z / z^α analytic on region containing contour
rubrics_metrics.description: When integrands involve log z or z^α, pick a branch of the logarithm that is analytic in a region including the contour (e.g., exclude the negative imaginary axis and take imaginary part in (π/2, 3π/2)). The region should be simply connected to make log single-valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a branch so that analytic continuation along the contour is possible; ensure the contour and region avoid the branch cut. The chosen branch affects residues and relations between values on positive and negative real axis (useful for relating integrals on (−∞,0) and (0,∞)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating arc integrals: bound integrand × arc length
rubrics_metrics.description: To show arc contributions vanish, bound the modulus of the integrand on the arc (e.g., by R^{deg P − deg Q} or by exponential decay) and multiply by the arc length; show this tends to 0 as R→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show using deg comparisons (polynomial ratios) or exponential decay (e^{i z} factors) to bound integrand; ensure uniform bounds on arc that produce vanishing as radius increases. For small semicircles around real poles, bound by supremum × arc length and let indentation radius →0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global Cauchy Integral Theorem (simply connected regions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a bounded simply connected region U, then ∮_Γ f(z) dz = 0 for every piecewise C^1 closed curve Γ in U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extends the disk-based Cauchy theorem to any bounded simply connected region. The result is used to derive global Cauchy integral formula, Argument Principle, and Residue Theorem. Boundedness is not essential but simplifies exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of simply connected (complement connected) and winding-number criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounded region U is simply connected iff its complement in C is connected. Equivalently (via Lemma B.39), U is simply connected iff n(Γ,a)=0 for all piecewise C^1 cycles Γ in U and all points a in C \ U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equivalence to the usual 'every loop can be contracted to a point' is shown via winding-number arguments. This criterion is used to ensure existence of single-valued logarithms and global integral results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chains and cycles formalism for line integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: A piecewise C^1 chain is a formal sum of piecewise C^1 curves; allowable operations include subdivision, fusion, reparametrization, cancellation/ insertion of opposite arcs, dropping/inserting one-point arcs. A chain is a cycle exactly when in any representation initial and endpoints occur in matching pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalism allows definition of line integrals over chains independent of representation and supports algebraic manipulations used in the global Cauchy theorem proof (e.g., grid decomposition into rectangles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Global Cauchy Integral Formula
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a simply connected region U and Γ is a piecewise C^1 cycle in U, and z∈U not on image(Γ), then (1/2πi) ∮_Γ f(ζ)/(ζ−z) dζ = n(Γ,z) f(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply global Cauchy theorem to g(ζ) = (f(ζ) − f(z))/(ζ−z) which is analytic in U after removing the removable singularity at ζ=z. Use winding number n(Γ,z) when Γ winds multiple times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of single-valued log f in simply connected region when f nowhere vanishing
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(z) is analytic and nowhere zero in bounded simply connected U, one can define an analytic single-valued branch of log f(z) on U by integrating f'/f along paths from a basepoint (since ∮ f'/f = 0 on closed curves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct F(z)=∫_{z0}^z f'/f and set log f(z) = log f(z0) + F(z). This relies on Theorem B.40 (global Cauchy) to ensure path-independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument Principle (global form)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a meromorphic f in simply connected U with zeros {a_j} of orders h_j and poles {b_l} of orders k_l, and Γ a piecewise C^1 cycle in U avoiding zeros/poles, (1/2πi) ∮_Γ f'(z)/f(z) dz = Σ_j h_j n(Γ,a_j) − Σ_l k_l n(Γ,b_l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This counts zeros and poles inside Γ with multiplicity weighted by winding number. Requires f meromorphic and Γ avoiding singularities; derived by applying global Cauchy theory to f'/f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue computation at simple poles via limit formula
rubrics_metrics.description: For a simple pole at a, Res f(a) = lim_{z→a} (z−a) f(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples compute residues at simple poles of rational or exponential-type functions using this limit. For higher order poles, use derivative formulas (not detailed on this chunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relating integrals using symmetry and branch relations; equate real parts
rubrics_metrics.description: When integrand uses log z or is even/odd, exploit symmetry and chosen branch relations between values on positive and negative real axis (e.g., log x vs log x + πi for negative x) to relate complex contour integrals to desired real integrals and extract real parts to compute them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show using the chosen log branch (excluding negative imaginary axis) to write integrals over contours and then equating real parts to obtain values like ∫_0^∞ log(1+x^2)/(1+x^2)^2 dx = π/2.
